pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 11–12 — understand and use place value for decimals, measures and integers of ANY size; extend the number system so all positive/negative integers, decimals and fractions sit on a single number line.
• Standards—UK (DfE NC Mathematics, KS3): 'understand and use place value for decimals, measures and integers of any size' and 'order positive and negative integers, decimals and fractions' on one line.
• Standards—US (CCSS-M): 6.NS.C.6 (position integers and rationals on the number line, opposites) and 6.NS.C.7 (understand ordering of rational numbers).
• Operational details: Consolidate the ×10/÷10 place-value structure as UNBOUNDED in both directions — no largest, no smallest place — and unify previously separate representations (whole numbers, decimals, negatives, fractions) onto ONE number line. Stress that every number, however written, names a single point; the line is the common ground where mixed forms can be compared.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 11): 'State the value of the 7 in 4,700,000 and in 0.007.' Tier B: 'Place −3/4, 0.6, −2 and 1.25 on one number line.' Tier C: 'Explain why the place-value system has no largest and no smallest place.'
bestPractices: Present place value as a single unbounded ×10/÷10 structure — no largest or smallest place — rather than a table that stops at millions or thousandths
Unify whole numbers, decimals, negatives and fractions onto ONE number line so mixed forms share a common reference for comparison
Insist every representation (numeral, fraction, decimal) names a single POINT on the line
Convert between forms to a common representation (usually decimal or a common denominator) before comparing across types
Use magnitude/scale reasoning ('the value of a digit is its face value times its place') for numbers of any size
keyRepresentations: Single number line hosting integers, decimals, negatives and fractions together
Place-value chart extended arbitrarily far left and right of the decimal point
Zoomable number line to locate decimals/fractions between integers
Form-conversion cards (fraction ↔ decimal) feeding points onto the line
commonMisconceptions: Thinking place value 'runs out' at a largest place (millions) or smallest place (thousandths)
Treating whole numbers, decimals, negatives and fractions as living on separate scales rather than one line
Placing negatives as if their magnitude sets their order (−3/4 to the left of −2)
Assuming a fraction and its decimal (3/4 and 0.75) are different points rather than the same point
Comparing mixed forms by surface features (digit count) rather than converting to a common form

learn.summary: For ages 11–12: extend place value as an unbounded ×10/÷10 structure (no largest or smallest place) and unify whole numbers, decimals, negatives and fractions onto ONE number line, where every number — however written — names a single point. Learners locate and order mixed forms by position relative to zero and to integer landmarks, recognising that a fraction and its decimal (e.g. 3/4 and 0.75) are the SAME point, and that on a standard (left-to-right) line ordering follows leftmost-is-smallest across all number types.

activities.title: Many forms, one line
feedback: If a fraction is placed by its visible digits (e.g. 1/2 put near the 2), convert it to a decimal or locate it between integer landmarks: 1/2 = 0.5 sits halfway between 0 and 1, not near 2.
If negatives are ordered by magnitude (e.g. −3/4 placed left of −2), anchor zero: on a standard line every point further left is smaller, so −2 < −3/4 because −2 is further from zero on the left.
If 3/4 and 0.75 are placed at different points, convert 3/4 to 0.75 and confirm both describe three-quarters of the way from 0 to 1 — they are literally one point.
activities.rationale: Placing mixed representations on a single line forces a common measure of size and confronts the misconceptions that different number types live on separate scales and that notation digits dictate position. This supports ordering integers, decimals and fractions on one line.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils understand and use place value for decimals, measures and integers of any size and order integers, decimals and fractions on a number line.
6.NS.C.6/C.7: position integers and rational numbers on the number line and understand ordering of rational numbers.
learnerActions: Draw a single number line and place each of these numbers on it: −3/4, 0.6, −2, and 1.25. Then, on a separate zoomed-out view using an appropriate scale, mark a large integer such as 4,700,000, noting that the same ×10/÷10 structure governs both views.
For each number, say in words where it sits relative to zero and to the nearest whole-number landmarks (e.g. '1.25 is a quarter of the way from 1 to 2').
Place 3/4 and 0.75 separately, then check that both land on exactly the same point; write one sentence explaining why they must coincide.

Write all the numbers in order from smallest to largest, treating 3/4 and 0.75 as one point, and justify the order using position on the line, not the digits (−2 < −3/4 < 0.6 < 3/4 = 0.75 < 1.25 < 4,700,000).
activities.intendedInsight: Whole numbers, decimals, negatives and fractions all belong to one number line governed by a single ×10/÷10 structure; each names a single point and equivalent forms name the same point. On a standard (left-to-right) line, size is read as position (leftmost is smallest) across every type, even when very large and very small values must be shown at different scales.

activities.title: Zoom in — is there a smallest place?
feedback: If the line is treated as discrete ('the next number', only a few slots between landmarks), zoom one segment and mark finer divisions to show more and more numbers fit — any fraction or decimal has a place.
If the learner claims place value 'runs out' at thousandths or at millions, point to the column-naming continuing with each zoom: the pattern is ×10/÷10 repeated, with no final column.
activities.rationale: Progressive subdivision makes the unbounded ×10/÷10 place-value structure concrete, addressing the misconception that place value stops at a largest or smallest place; it also illustrates (informally) that the line keeps subdividing so any decimal or fraction has a place.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils understand and use place value for decimals, measures and integers of any size and order integers, decimals and fractions on a number line.
learnerActions: Take the segment from 0 to 1 and subdivide it into tenths; label 0.6 among them.
Zoom into a tenth (e.g. between 0.6 and 0.7) and subdivide into hundredths; place a value such as 0.65.
Zoom again into hundredths and mark thousandths; keep a note of which place column you are in at each step (tenths → hundredths → thousandths…).
Argue in writing whether this subdividing ever stops, and state what that means for a 'smallest place' in the place-value system.
Repeat the reasoning outward: explain why there is likewise no largest place as the ×10 structure grows.
activities.intendedInsight: The ×10/÷10 place-value structure continues without end in both directions — there is no smallest place and no largest place. Informally, between any two points more numbers can always be found, so any decimal or fraction has a location between landmarks.

activities.title: Value of a digit at any scale
feedback: If only the face value (7) is given, prompt for the place: the 7 in 4,700,000 is 7 hundred-thousands = 700,000; the 7 in 0.007 is 7 thousandths = 0.007.
If columns are miscounted on the decimal side, count rightward from the decimal point: tenths, hundredths, thousandths.
activities.rationale: Magnitude/scale reasoning for digits of any size consolidates place value as a single unbounded structure rather than a table that stops at millions or thousandths.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils understand and use place value for decimals, measures and integers of any size and order integers, decimals and fractions on a number line.
learnerActions: State the value of the 7 in 4,700,000 and the value of the 7 in 0.007.
For each, say which place column the 7 occupies and compute face value × place value.
Explain in one or two sentences why the same digit can represent vastly different amounts depending on its place.
Optional extension: explain to a partner (or in writing) why the place-value system has no largest and no smallest place.
activities.intendedInsight: A digit's value is its face value times its place value, and this scaling reasoning works for numbers of any size, large or small.

activities.title: Which is smaller, and why
feedback: Correct ordering: −3 < 1/2 < 2.75. −3 is smallest because it is furthest left of zero, regardless of number type.
If 1/2 is ranked below −3 ('it's less than one'), anchor zero: every negative lies left of every positive, so −3 < 1/2 whatever the digits suggest.
If 2.75 is ranked by '275', relocate it as three-quarters of the way from 2 to 3 and compare positions.
activities.rationale: This diagnostic comparison exposes ordering-by-magnitude-of-negatives and reading-by-digits, and the justification for '−3 smallest' reveals whether the learner reasons by position across types.
sourceClaims: 6.NS.C.6/C.7: position integers and rational numbers on the number line and understand ordering of rational numbers.
learnerActions: Place −3, 1/2 and 2.75 on one number line relative to zero and to each other.
Order them from smallest to largest.
Explain how you know −3 is the smallest, referring to its position rather than the size of the digit 3.
Name a number between 1/2 and 2.75, and then another number between those two, to show many values lie between any pair.
activities.intendedInsight: On a standard (left-to-right) number line, across all number types the leftmost position (furthest below zero) is smallest; a negative can be smaller than a small positive fraction even though its digit looks large. Informally, infinitely many numbers also lie between any two points.

constraints: Learners should construct placements and justifications themselves; multiple-choice or slider checks can consolidate the unified-line idea afterwards, but recognition-only responses do not elicit the independent placing, converting and justifying that evidences full understanding.

When comparing mixed forms, convert to a common representation (decimal or common denominator) or locate each between integer landmarks before ordering; do not compare by surface features such as digit count. Fractions remain comparable numbers; the common-reference requirement is about positioning represented portions consistently.

A static, annotated line showing several forms on one axis can illustrate the unification and is a useful scaffold, but it cannot be re-scaled by the learner, so pair it with hands-on subdividing/zooming when demonstrating that the structure is unbounded and that more numbers always fit between landmarks.

Treat large integers and sub-unit decimals at appropriate separate scales when a single drawn line cannot show both; the point is that the same ×10/÷10 structure governs each, so the unification is conceptual even when two views are used.
The number system here is one-dimensional, so a single line is the correct representation; avoid adding extra spatial dimensions that would misrepresent ordering.

'Leftmost is smallest' assumes the conventional left-to-right orientation of the number line; use that standard orientation and make it explicit rather than treating it as an intrinsic property of the numbers.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the two cited standards were marked verified:false in the source and have not been re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Source value-of-digit example checked: the 7 in 4,700,000 is 700,000 (7 hundred-thousands) and the 7 in 0.007 is 7 thousandths; both are internally consistent and retained.

Ordering checked: −3 < 1/2 < 2.75 and −2 < −3/4 < 0.6 < 1.25 < 4,700,000 are correct; the source's own stated misconception 'placing −3/4 left of −2' is correctly treated as an error to correct, not taught.

The subdividing/zoom demonstration illustrates (does not formally prove) the unbounded place-value structure and that numbers always lie between any two points; density is a true mathematical property but is not attributed to the cited standards, which support ordering and place value rather than density.
Optional interaction examples (zoomable/subdividing line, slider placement, snapping equivalent forms to one point, place-value read-out) are preserved as illustrative, not mandatory mechanisms.

probeDeeper: Why is −3 to the left of 1/2 when 3 is bigger than a half?
How did you decide exactly where 2.75 goes between the whole numbers?
Is 1/2 the same point as 0.5 on this line? How do you know?
Name a number between 1/2 and 2.75 — and another between those two.
assess.correctAnswer: −3 sits three to the LEFT of zero; 1/2 halfway between 0 and 1; 2.75 three-quarters of the way from 2 to 3. Ordered: −3 < 1/2 < 2.75. −3 is smallest because it is furthest left / below zero, regardless of the type of number.

errorPatterns.pattern: Orders negatives by magnitude — argues 1/2 is the smallest 'because it's less than one', and −3 is not really small because 3 is a decent-sized number.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor zero on the line; show every negative lies left of every positive, so −3 < any positive including 1/2, whatever the digits say.
errorPatterns.distractor: 1/2 is the smallest, because it's less than one.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child ranks 1/2 below −3, or is surprised −3 is least.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads a fraction/decimal by its visible digits — places 1/2 near 2, or ranks 2.75 by '275'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Convert to a common frame (all as decimals, or all located between integer landmarks) so 1/2 = 0.5 lands between 0 and 1, not near 2.
errorPatterns.distractor: 1/2 goes near the 2 on the line.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Placement or ordering tracks a digit in the notation rather than the number's value.

errorPatterns.pattern: Consecutive-number thinking — believes there is a 'next' number and only a few values sit between landmarks, so a fraction has one fixed slot with gaps around it.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Zoom a segment (0 to 1) and mark tenths, then hundredths, to show the line is dense — any decimal or fraction has a place.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child treats the line as discrete, unsure where non-integers 'fit' or claims spots are 'taken'.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot place mixed types on one line; orders by digits or by magnitude of negatives.
responseLevels.full: Locates and orders integers, fractions and decimals on a single line by position relative to zero and to integer landmarks, and justifies size by leftmost-is-smallest across all types.
responseLevels.partial: Places and orders correctly when types are separated, but muddles when integers, fractions and decimals must be compared together, or reverts to magnitude for the negative.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: On one number line you have to place −3, 1/2 and 2.75. Where does each go relative to zero and to each other — and how do you know −3 is the smallest?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Placing mixed representations on ONE line forces a common measure of size. A child with full place-value/number-system understanding orders across integers, fractions and decimals by position. A child who orders negatives by magnitude, or who cannot locate a fraction/decimal without a whole-number cue, is exposed — and the reason for '−3 smallest' is the tell.

sources.claim: KS3 pupils understand and use place value for decimals, measures and integers of any size and order integers, decimals and fractions on a number line.
